protocol.legal_basis: Authorisation page (p2): 'Community Pharmacy Expanded Scope of Practice Initiative. In accordance with regulation 17A of the Controlled Substances (Poisons) Regulations 2011 (the Poisons Regulations) a pharmacist is authorised to prescribe a prescription drug (not being a drug of dependence) if the pharmacist is included on the register of authorised pharmacists and the drug is prescribed in accordance with the Community Pharmacist Prescribing Code.' Vaccination administration is governed by (p10): 'All vaccinations must be administered in accordance with: the Australian Immunisation Handbook; the individual vaccine information provided by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) and aligned with current Australian Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation (ATAGI) advice.'
protocol.supervision_model: Document does not use 'collaborative'/'autonomous' terminology; its own wording (p2): an authorised pharmacist who 'is included on the register of authorised pharmacists' prescribing 'in accordance with the Community Pharmacist Prescribing Code'. Discretion clause (p6): 'When applying the information contained within this clinical practice guideline, pharmacists are advised to exercise professional discretion and judgement. The clinical practice guideline does not override the responsibility of the pharmacist to make decisions appropriate to the circumstances of the individual, in consultation with the patient and/or their carer.' p9: 'Pharmacists must use their professional judgement and consider the traveller's itinerary, personal characteristics and medical history when determining the need for referral to a medical practitioner/travel medicine clinic.' Delegation: rabies vaccine prescribing per the Australian Immunisation Handbook and Australian Medicines Handbook (p10); antimalarial chemoprophylaxis per Therapeutic Guidelines: Prophylaxis of malaria (p14); travellers' diarrhoea pharmacotherapy per Therapeutic Guidelines (p12); VTE prophylaxis pharmacotherapy requires medical-practitioner referral (p19).
protocol.scope_summary: SA Health (Community Pharmacy Expanded Scope of Practice Initiative) clinical practice guideline for pharmacist-delivered pre-travel health services: 'The primary purpose of the pre-travel health consultation is to minimise the traveller's risk of injury and illness by providing advice, education, vaccinations, medicines and/or medical kits tailored to each individual's personal and itinerary risks (8-11).' Covers the two 'Refer when' referral lists (p4-p5), key points, the comprehensive pre-travel risk assessment (Table 1), high-risk travellers, prevention and management of travel-related conditions (vaccination, rabies Table 2, travellers' diarrhoea Table 3, malaria Table 4, altitude illness Table 5, VTE Table 6), medical kits, travelling with medications, travel health education and counselling, patient resources, confirmation that management is appropriate, clinical review (post-travel review 'generally not required'), pharmacist resources and Appendix 1 references. Page 3 'Guideline Overview' contains no extractable body text; no age-based service restriction is printed anywhere in the extractable text. Few drug regimens are printed (rabies pre-exposure prophylaxis 3-dose schedule days 0, 7 and 28; named but undosed standby/prophylaxis agents); most dosing is delegated to Therapeutic Guidelines and the Australian Medicines Handbook.

steps.description: Gather information and assess patient's needs — patient history component of the comprehensive pre-travel risk assessment (Table 1, p7): 'Sufficient information should be obtained from the patient to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines.' Patient history should cover: age; pregnancy (current or planned) and breastfeeding status (if applicable); medical history including past and current conditions — conditions that influence susceptibility/severity of infections or immunocompromise (e.g., splenectomy, steroid/immunosuppressant therapy, active or recent cancer); conditions that may cause acute illness or require emergency treatment while overseas (e.g., asthma, diabetes, severe allergies and past allergic reactions); conditions increasing susceptibility to hypoxia (e.g., cardiorespiratory disease, severe anaemia) with importance based on destination; mental illness and current psychological state; chronic conditions (e.g., rheumatologic disorders); colostomy or ileostomy; disability or impairment; conditions that may impact on effectiveness or safety of malarial prophylaxis (e.g., previous malaria, central nervous system disease or cardiac conditions); ongoing hormone treatment (e.g., estrogen therapy, oral contraceptive pill, menopausal hormone therapy); thrombophilic conditions; history of venous thromboembolism (VTE); recent surgery or injury; recent cardiopulmonary and/or cerebrovascular event; current medications (particularly medications that may be prohibited in other countries, require supporting documentation, or require advice to be taken safely across time zones); allergies/adverse drug reactions, including allergies to vaccines; alcohol and drug history (considering destination regulations); smoking status; immunisation history (routine and travel vaccinations); obesity (body mass index (BMI)). Reminder (p9): 'Pharmacists can access a range of clinical information in a patient's My Health Record, including details about current and past medication history, allergies and current medical conditions.'

steps.description: Travel history, itinerary and travel details, plus high-risk traveller review (Table 1, p7-p9). Travel history: 'Previous travel experience, including: experience with chemoprophylaxis for malaria; experience at high altitudes (if applicable to destination); VTE prophylaxis; experience with travel-related and other relevant illnesses.' Itinerary and travel details: countries and regions in itinerary (remoteness; access and quality of medical facilities; hygiene; epidemiology of infectious diseases; season and likely weather conditions); duration of total trip and duration of stay in each area; reason for travel (e.g., leisure, 'health tourism', international development or aid work); planned activities (e.g., snow sports, scuba diving, moped/vehicle use, disaster relief, long distance walking or cycling); travel style (mode of transport and travel times e.g., cruise ships, long-haul flights; backpacking, guided tours; traveller risk tolerance; accommodation type). High risk travellers (p8-p9): 'Specific personal characteristics or complex itineraries may put some travellers at an increased risk of illness or require special consideration, including for the purposes of travel insurance and certification to fly, including (11): travellers with chronic conditions (medical practitioner assessment may be required); travellers with risk factors for VTE (referral to a medical practitioner required for patients at moderate to high risk of VTE); immunocompromised travellers ... (referral to a medical practitioner is required) (10); pregnant women (referral to a specialist travel medicine clinic and/or usual pregnancy care provider is required); young children (referral to a specialist travel medicine clinic/medical practitioner is required for all children < 2 years, and may be required for other children, depending on itinerary); the elderly or immobile (medical practitioner assessment may be required for travel insurance purposes for adults aged ≥ 65 years); travellers with disabilities; travellers on extended trips particularly to developing countries where medical care is relatively unavailable; backpackers and travellers visiting friends and relatives (risks are often underestimated in these groups); planned high risk sexual activities (e.g., engaging with sex workers, group sex).'

'Pharmacists should review a patient's vaccination record using the Australian Immunisation Register (AIR) (Note: A patient's AIR record may not display all of the vaccines they have previously received, as the AIR only started to hold vaccination records for people aged over 7 years from 2016, and mandatory reporting of administered vaccines to the AIR was rolled out even more recently ...)' steps.description: Condition-specific risk stratification against Tables 2 to 6 before any prescribing. Rabies (Table 2, p10): pre-exposure prophylaxis recommended for people travelling to rabies-enzootic regions based on a risk assessment considering 'the patient's risk of rabies exposure and the patient's access to emergency medical attention in that location'. Travellers' diarrhoea (Table 3, p11-p12): patient risk factors 'Travellers with comorbidities such as diabetes, heart failure, bowel abnormalities, cancer, HIV or immunosuppression and elderly travellers are at increased risk. The very young are more likely to have severe disease. Travellers aged between 15-29 years and backpackers are at increased risk predominantly due to travel style.' Malaria (Table 4, p13): 'Travellers at risk of severe disease must be referred to a medical practitioner'; pharmacotherapy considerations include destination(s) and seasons, patterns of antimalarial resistance, individual risk of mosquito bites, individual risk of severe malarial illness, risk of adverse effects and drug toxicity and ability to swallow the prescribed prophylaxis, potential for resistance, and the efficacy of each drug (2, 10, 11). Altitude (Table 5, p15-p17): altitude assumed to start at 1,200m; elevations above 1,500m considered high altitude; highest risk above 2,500m though it may occur from 1,500m; low/moderate/high-risk ascent categories for unacclimatised individuals; 'Referral point: Travellers with a history of altitude illness or at moderate or high risk of AMS must be referred ...'. VTE (Table 6, p18-p19): risk factors as listed; 'Travellers with one or more additional risk factors for VTE ... should have their risk estimated using a VTE risk calculator, such as the Padua Prediction Score for Risk of VTE (25) and be referred to a medical practitioner if VTE prophylaxis is indicated'; long-distance travel defined as 'travel by air, road or rail of 4 hours duration or greater', particularly air travel ≥ 8 hours.

steps.description: Preventive and management measures, immunisation plan and pharmacotherapy (p6, p9-p20). Components of the consultation: 'immunisation and development of an immunisation plan; venous thromboembolism; travel related illnesses e.g., malaria and other mosquito-borne diseases, travellers' diarrhoea, rabies, altitude sickness, sexually transmitted infections; planned activities; The need for appropriate travel insurance; Requirements of a medical kit; Required documentation ...'. Rabies: 'Pre-exposure prophylaxis is recommended as a 3-dose schedule, administered on days 0, 7 and 28.' 'Where pre-exposure prophylaxis is recommended, the pharmacist must prescribe the rabies vaccine in accordance with the Australian Immunisation Handbook: Rabies and other lyssaviruses and the Australian Medicines Handbook (18, 32). The dispensed medicine may then be administered.' Travellers' diarrhoea (p11-p12): 'Rehydration is the mainstay of therapy for travellers' diarrhoea'; 'No treatment is required for mild, short episodes. Antimotility drugs may be considered for self-treatment for adults and children >12 years who do not have bloody stools or fever (loperamide is preferred).'; 'Most cases of travellers' diarrhoea do not require antibiotics; self-initiated treatment with antibiotics may be acceptable for acute, moderate to severe diarrhoea only (diarrhoea that is distressing, incapacitating, interferes with or completely prevents planned activities or dysentery (bloody stools))NB1 (33).'; 'Stand-by pharmacotherapy may be provided as part of a medical kit: Antibiotics in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Travellers' diarrhoea (1) Recommended treatments include azithromycin, norfloxacin and ciprofloxacin as single dose therapy; and Antidiarrhoeal drugs in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antidiarrhoeal drugs for acute gastroenteritis (3); and Oral antiemetics for the treatment of acute nausea and vomiting associated with gastroenteritis in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal: Nausea and vomiting (Antiemetic drugs in adults) (6).' Malaria (p14): 'If required, antimalarial chemoprophylaxis may be prescribed in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Prophylaxis of malaria (2). Atorvaquone with proguanil or doxycycline may be used as per guidelines. Stand-by emergency treatment should be prescribed to people travelling to malaria-endemic areas who choose not to use chemoprophylaxis as part of a medical kit (for when emergency medical care cannot be obtained within 24 hours) ...' Altitude (p17-p18): 'Travellers at low risk of altitude illness generally do not require pharmacological prophylaxis. General treatment for altitude illness includes stopping, resting and rehydrating; the most effective treatment is descent. Standby treatment may be prescribed for adults for the initial management of altitude illness as part of a medical kit (with appropriate instructions for use in the event the person cannot seek immediate medical care or descend) to people at low risk of altitude illness travelling to elevations >2,500m in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: General treatment for altitude illness and specific drug treatments for AMS and HACE (4).' steps.description: Travel health education and counselling (p21-p22): 'Comprehensive advice and counselling (including supporting written information when required) should be provided to the patient regarding: individual product and medicine use, including dosing and indications; how to manage adverse effects; accessing medications, treatment and health advice; seeking medical care and/or treatment post travel for ongoing issues.' 'Travellers should be counselled and provided with advice to enable safe travel and risk minimisation (11).' 'Travellers should be advised to sign up for Smartraveller subscriber alerts for up-to-date information about health risks.' Common topics for all travellers: 'emerging health issues and diseases relevant to the traveller; appropriate travel insurance; personal safety.' Other topics (as applicable): choosing safe food and drinks; insect and other pest avoidance; avoiding environmental exposures (contaminated soil and water); dog or other animal bite management; injuries including aquatic and traffic accidents; alcohol and drug use; weather conditions and potential for natural disasters; prevention of VTE; availability of counterfeit medications or supplements; safe sex practices; blood borne infections (acquired through cosmetic/medical procedures, tattoos, piercings and intravenous drug use); altitude illness and the importance of planned gradual ascent; staying safe in conflicts or situations of civil unrest; motion sickness; jet lag; international driving licences. Travelling with medications (p21): 'People planning to take any type of medication or supplements overseas ... particularly controlled substances (e.g., Vyvanse® (lisdexamfetamine), must confirm any restrictions and requirements/permits with the destination country's embassy or consulate.' 'All medicines should be carried in their original packaging, clearly labelled with the contents, patient name and dose; travellers should be advised not to use pillboxes (10).' 'Medications should be packed in carry-on luggage and an extra supply should be included in the event the trip is extended (10).' Rabies general advice (Table 2, p10): 'Advise travellers, especially those with young children, to avoid contact with wild and domestic animals including stray dogs and cats ... Avoid contact with bats anywhere in the world. Provide education about treatment for potential rabies exposure including first aid and requirement for post-exposure prophylaxis vaccine and, in some cases, human rabies immunoglobulin.' Malaria general advice (Table 4, p13): mosquito avoidance — 'Prevention through use of effective insect repellent, other insecticide products and mosquito nets, remaining indoors from dusk to dawn where possible, wearing long trousers and long-sleeved shirts in the evening and avoiding strong fragrances.' Altitude preventive advice (p17): gradual ascent — 'take at least 2 days to ascend to 3,000m; do not increase sleeping altitude by more than 500m per day if above 3,000m; allow an extra day for acclimatisation every 1,000m' plus 'all symptoms at high altitude should be considered altitude sickness until determined otherwise; seek medical care as soon as signs or symptoms are experienced; never ascend to a higher altitude to sleep with symptoms of altitude sickness; do not leave a person with suspected altitude illness alone; always attempt to descend if symptoms are severe or worsen'. VTE preventive measures (p19): remaining ambulant before and after travel; regular movement during travel such as thigh and calf stretching exercises; adequate legroom; avoiding alcohol and sedatives before and during travel; wearing loose clothing.

open_questions.topic: Page 3 'Guideline Overview' contains no extractable body text
open_questions.observed: Page 3 extracts as the heading 'Guideline Overview' plus the page footer only.
open_questions.why_unclear: Any overview eligibility statement printed as a graphic on p3 could not be read; inclusion criteria were built from the extractable prose (p5-p9). No age-based service restriction appears anywhere in the extractable text.

open_questions.topic: No service age restriction is printed — age_bounds left null
open_questions.observed: Ages appear only as referral triggers: children < 2 years; children ≤ 8 years (altitude >2,500m, malaria prophylaxis/stand-by); adults ≥ 65 years (malaria prophylaxis/stand-by); VTE risk factor 'older age (≥ 70 years)'; diarrhoea risk 'travellers aged between 15-29 years'; National Lung-Cancer-style bands absent; altitude standby treatment 'for adults'.
open_questions.why_unclear: These are referral thresholds rather than service eligibility bounds, so age_bounds is null/null with provenance on p4 and this record, per spec notes.

open_questions.topic: Combinatorics of inclusion criteria not printed
open_questions.observed: The guideline states consultation components and referral requirements but never labels inclusion criteria as AND/OR.
open_questions.why_unclear: Defaulted to {all_of: [INC-1..INC-6]} per spec rule 4; INC-1 and INC-6 are derived with confidence 'medium'.

open_questions.topic: Table 5 (altitude patient risk factors) is a two-column list that interleaves in text extraction
open_questions.observed: p15 rows alternate between the left column (e.g. Cardiovascular disorders, Obesity, Chronic kidney disease) and the right column (e.g. Neurological disorders, Ophthalmic conditions) in the extracted reading order.
open_questions.why_unclear: Condition-to-category assignment was reconstructed from reading order; EXC-36 and RF-36 carry confidence 'medium' and the full flat list should be verified against the PDF page image.

open_questions.topic: Low/moderate/high-risk ascent table (p16-p17) is garbled in extraction
open_questions.observed: The three-column table ('Low risk | Moderate risk | High risk') mixes fragments across columns, e.g. '> No history of AMS ascending to ≤ 2,800m', '> Ascents taking ≥ 2 days to reach 2,500m-3,000m, with further increases in sleeping elevation to a maximum of 500m per day ...'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Row-to-column assignment cannot be recovered reliably from text; the risk categories are referenced by EXC-39/RF-39 but individual thresholds were not transcribed into structured fields. Verify against the PDF.

open_questions.topic: Most drug doses are delegated to external guidelines
open_questions.observed: Rabies vaccine schedule printed (days 0, 7 and 28) but no brand/strength/route; travellers' diarrhoea antibiotics 'in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Travellers' diarrhoea' with only 'single dose therapy' printed; antimalarials 'as per guidelines'; VTE prophylaxis agents named without doses; altitude standby treatment and antiemetics delegated.
open_questions.why_unclear: Dose/strength fields left empty rather than invented; TX-2 to TX-16 carry empty dose fields by design.

open_questions.observed: p14: 'Atorvaquone with proguanil or doxycycline may be used as per guidelines.'
open_questions.why_unclear: The standard spelling is 'atovaquone'; transcribed exactly as printed with confidence 'medium' and flagged rather than silently corrected.

open_questions.observed: Primary referral lists p4-p5; vaccination referrals p9-p10; diarrhoea p12; malaria p13-p14; altitude p15, p17; VTE p18-p19; post-travel advice p23.
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec requires one shared provenance for the referral block; page 4 (first page) used, full range recorded here.

open_questions.observed: 'is required for' and 'must be referred' wording appears without any timeframe, except 'immediate referral is required if malaria is suspected'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Routine vs urgent classification is therefore derived from the document's own adverbs ('required', 'must', 'immediate'); no numeric timeframe could be transcribed.

open_questions.topic: 'Adults' for altitude standby treatment is undefined
open_questions.observed: 'Standby treatment may be prescribed for adults for the initial management of altitude illness ... to people at low risk of altitude illness travelling to elevations >2,500m'.
open_questions.why_unclear: No numeric adult age is printed (the guideline elsewhere uses ≥ 65 years and ≤ 8 years bands); the age at which an adult qualifies for altitude standby treatment is not stated.

open_questions.topic: VTE risk-criterion thresholds are printed as risk factors, not referral triggers
open_questions.observed: 'previous history of VTE; reduced mobility (at least 3 days); older age (≥ 70 years); ... chemotherapy or radiotherapy within the previous 6 months; recent trauma/surgery (within previous month)' are listed as factors 'that may indicate the need for pharmacologic prophylaxis'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Only 'one or more additional risk factors' plus a Padua estimate triggers referral (EXC-40); individual thresholds retained inside the criterion text rather than as separate red flags.

open_questions.topic: Mapping of printed urgency language to severity values
open_questions.observed: 'medical emergency and requires immediate descent' (HACE/HAPE) → critical/REFER_URGENT; 'emergency treatment must be sought for febrile illness' and 'immediate referral is required if malaria is suspected' → high/REFER_URGENT; 'is required for'/'must be referred' → medium/REFER; 'may be required' → medium/REVIEW_GP or REFER; consultation-component referral → low.
open_questions.why_unclear: No numeric severity scale is printed; mapping recorded so it can be re-checked.

open_questions.topic: Yellow fever, Q fever and BCG referral specifics
open_questions.observed: 'Yellow fever vaccine – see Approved Yellow Fever Vaccination Providers in SA (28)'; 'Q fever vaccine – see Approved Q Fever Vaccination Providers in SA (29)'; 'BCG vaccine – the BCG vaccine is only provided through the SA Tuberculosis Service, see SA Tuberculosis services in CALHN for further information on referral (30)'.
open_questions.why_unclear: The provider lists themselves are external documents (references 28-30) and are not reproduced in this guideline.

open_questions.topic: National Lung Cancer Screening Program-style criteria not present; screening content limited to AIR and immunity testing
open_questions.observed: Vaccination section covers AIR review and laboratory testing for immunity but no other screening programme is mentioned in this guideline.
open_questions.why_unclear: No content issue — recorded to make clear that no additional programme eligibility rules were invented for this document.

open_questions.topic: Gate on_fail values not stated by the document for most steps
open_questions.observed: The guideline prints referral requirements but no explicit branch outcomes for incomplete history, declined testing or failed confirmation checks.
open_questions.why_unclear: Used SEE_PW-1-S5 to route into referral triage, STOP for confirm-management and vaccination-compliance failures, REFER/REFER_URGENT for mandatory and immediate referrals, and 'unclear' where the document states no consequence (spec rule 5).

open_questions.topic: 'Stand-by' vs 'standby' spelling varies in the document
open_questions.observed: 'stand-by treatment' (p4, p5), 'Stand-by pharmacotherapy' (p12), 'standby treatment' (p11, Table 3), 'Standby treatment' (p17-p18).
open_questions.why_unclear: Transcribed as printed in each quoted string; no harmonisation applied.

open_questions.observed: p21: 'particularly controlled substances (e.g., Vyvanse® (lisdexamfetamine), must confirm any restrictions and requirements/permits with the destination country's embassy or consulate.'
open_questions.why_unclear: The example is a medication-travel logistics instruction, not a prescribing rule; captured verbatim in the EDUCATE step rather than as a treatment row.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Content of page 3 'Guideline Overview' (no extractable text) — confirm it contains no eligibility or age-restriction statement.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Eligibility for this guideline is otherwise undefined; any printed scope statement would change INC/age_bounds.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Dose regimens (strength, dose, route, frequency, duration, max dose) for rabies vaccine, travellers' diarrhoea antibiotics, antimalarial chemoprophylaxis and stand-by emergency treatment, altitude standby treatment, antiemetics, and VTE prophylaxis from the referenced Therapeutic Guidelines and the Australian Medicines Handbook.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Only the rabies schedule (days 0, 7 and 28) and 'single dose therapy' are printed; all other dose fields are empty and must be filled before go-live.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Correction/confirmation of the printed spelling 'Atorvaquone with proguanil' (standard: atovaquone with proguanil) and the product/strength to be dispensed.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Transcribed as printed with confidence 'medium'; the engine should use the confirmed generic name.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Operational thresholds for the altitude risk categories (low/moderate/high-risk ascents table, p16-p17) taken from the PDF page image.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The three-column table is garbled in text extraction; EXC-39/RF-39 depend on correctly assigning a traveller's ascent profile to a risk category.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Verification of the Table 5 (altitude pre-existing conditions) two-column layout against the PDF page image.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: EXC-36/RF-36 were reconstructed from an interleaved extraction and carry confidence 'medium'; referral decisions depend on the list.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Referral destinations, contact details and timeframes for each referral class (specialised travel medicine clinic, sexual health clinic or GP, usual medical practitioner, approved yellow fever/Q fever providers, SA Tuberculosis Service), including after-hours arrangements.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Destinations are partly named with no contact details or timeframes; local pathways must be configured.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Local scope decisions: which travel vaccines this pharmacy may administer (the guideline names yellow fever, Q fever and BCG as not endorsed in the community pharmacy setting), and any SA-specific approved-provider lists.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: 'Not endorsed for administration in the community pharmacy setting' is asserted without a printed list beyond the three named vaccines.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Whether VTE prophylaxis pharmacotherapy is absolutely outside pharmacist scope — 'Travellers requiring pharmacotherapy for VTE prophylaxis must be referred to a medical practitioner' (aspirin, rivaroxaban, apixaban, enoxaparin named as options).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The drugs are listed as prophylaxis options while referral is mandatory; the boundary between advice and supply must be confirmed.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Definition of 'adults' for altitude standby treatment eligibility.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: No numeric age is printed; the rule cannot be evaluated by the engine without one.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Operational cut-off for 'longer than 8 weeks' in malaria-endemic areas and 'duration of stay in each area' accounting (multi-country itineraries).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The referral trigger depends on cumulative vs per-country duration, which the document does not define.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Malaria stand-by emergency treatment dispensing rule — 'for when emergency medical care cannot be obtained within 24 hours' — and what evidence the pharmacist records that this condition applies.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: A supply condition is printed but its verification and documentation are not.

hugh_to_confirm.item: ICV (yellow card) issuance process — who may complete it, record-keeping and fee, given 'The ICV can be completed by any practitioner authorised to give vaccinations'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Obligation is printed with no process detail.

hugh_to_confirm.item: AIR upload timing and content for travel vaccines, including handling of patients whose AIR record is incomplete (AIR only holds records for people aged over 7 years from 2016).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Upload is required but timing/fields are not printed, and the AIR limitation is printed without a workaround rule.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Operational compliance evidence for each prescribing event: pharmacist 'included on the register of authorised pharmacists' and prescribing 'in accordance with the Community Pharmacist Prescribing Code' (regulation 17A, Controlled Substances (Poisons) Regulations 2011).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Legal basis is stated but the record-keeping/verification steps are not; local process must be confirmed before go-live.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Post-travel advice script and documentation — 'Clinical review with the pharmacist post travel is generally not required' while referral rules apply for persisting symptoms; confirm what the pharmacist must record at the pre-travel consult about post-travel escalation.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The tension between 'generally not required' review and mandatory post-travel referral needs an operational rule.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Whether the discretion clauses (p6, p9) permit deviation from any 'is required for'/'must be referred' trigger, or only from advisory wording.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: 'Pharmacists must use their professional judgement ... when determining the need for referral' sits alongside mandatory referral language; the hierarchy must be decided locally.
